blocks.text: MS SHELLEY TOMLINS (affirmed) (via video link)
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Examination-in-chief by MR ASTBURY
Could we start with your full name, please?
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, Shelley Anne Tomlins.
blocks.speaker: TOMLINS

blocks.text: Thank you. Your profession, please, Ms Tomlins?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Full-time student at the moment, but still a registered nurse.
blocks.speaker: TOMLINS

blocks.text: Thank you. Were you employed in that capacity at the Countess of Chester Hospital between April 2011 and October 2015?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, I was.
blocks.speaker: TOMLINS

blocks.text: Were you at that time a band 5 staff nurse?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: TOMLINS

blocks.text: But had you completed additional qualifications specific to neonatal nursing?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, I completed the introduction to neonatal nursing and the special intensive care of the newborn in Liverpool.
blocks.speaker: TOMLINS

blocks.text: Thank you. I'm going to ask you, please, about two day shifts that you completed on the 4th and 5 August 2015.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Okay.
blocks.speaker: TOMLINS

blocks.text: I appreciate, when you provided a statement to the police, you relied on the notes that had been made available to you; is that right?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: TOMLINS

blocks.text: So largely I'm going to take you through the notes, but we'll pause and try to recall some detail at certain points.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Okay.
blocks.speaker: TOMLINS

blocks.text: Thank you. So if we could begin, please, with 4 August 2015. The jury will hear that your colleague, [Nurse B], was the designated nurse during that shift for [Baby F], about whom I'm going to be asking you.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Okay.
blocks.speaker: TOMLINS

blocks.text: I'm going to ask that tile 64 be put on the screen. If we can look at that, please, the underlying material.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Can you see that clearly, Ms Tomlins?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, I can.
blocks.speaker: TOMLINS

blocks.text: Thank you. An observation chart, as you can see, in the name of [Baby F], dated from the 3rd into 4 August of 2015.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Okay.
blocks.speaker: TOMLINS

blocks.text: If we can scroll down, please, to the bottom row. I'm going to ask if you can see your initials anywhere in any column.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes. It's in one of them.
blocks.speaker: TOMLINS

blocks.text: Perhaps if you could tell us -- is it -- if we look about two-thirds across to the right, we can see, bearing in mind your introduction, "SAT".
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, that's me.
blocks.speaker: TOMLINS

blocks.text: If we scroll up that column we can see that that entry was made at 10 am on 4 August.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: TOMLINS

blocks.text: As we scroll down the column, can you confirm, please, that the entries that you've made on each occasion fall within what we understand from this chart are the acceptable levels for a neonate?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, they do.
blocks.speaker: TOMLINS

blocks.text: Thank you. In a similar vein, please, if we can go to tile number 66. Again, if we can perhaps just concentrate initially on the row at the bottom of the left-hand page. Is this another form that you'll be familiar with from your time in Chester?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes. That's the ICU observation chart. It's small but I can see myself again in the 10 am column, I think, yes.
blocks.speaker: TOMLINS

blocks.text: Thank you. That's what I was about to ask you.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Thank you very much.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: If we go up the column, can you confirm they are entries that you made in respect of various equipment settings and readings in relation to [Baby F]'s treatment?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, I made those entries.
blocks.speaker: TOMLINS

blocks.text: So would that be consistent with you perhaps assisting [Nurse B] with [Baby F]'s observations at around 10 o'clock in the morning on that day shift?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: TOMLINS

blocks.text: We're going to move on, please, to 5 August, another day shift that you worked. We understand that would have been between 7.30 in the morning and 8 in the evening.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: TOMLINS

blocks.text: Again, did you rely on the medical notes that were made available to you to compile the statement that you provided to the police?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I did, yes. I had pretty much no memory of that particular day.
blocks.speaker: TOMLINS

blocks.text: Thank you. If we go first, please, to tile 212. I hope you'll see a representation of the start of your day shift. So the designated nurse for [Baby F], were you able to confirm that from the notes?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, I was, yes.
blocks.speaker: TOMLINS

blocks.text: Thank you. If we go to the next tile, please, and we look at the material behind it. I'm going to ask Mr Murphy, please, to zoom in on your entry at 8 am.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I think in fact they're to the right, if I recall, of the forms as opposed to the left, sorry. That first paragraph.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So again, this is a form which I'm sure you're familiar with, Ms Tomlins, and I think we're becoming familiar with. These are the nursing notes that you would enter from time to time on a computer system known as Meditech; is that right?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, that's right.
blocks.speaker: TOMLINS

blocks.text: If we look along the second line of text in the box, created 5 August 15, 08.40. Then a second time, 8.42.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: From your recollection, would that show the time the note started and ended by way of input to the computer?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I think so, yes. I can't be sure, but that seems logical. It'd take about 2 minutes.
blocks.speaker: TOMLINS

blocks.text: We can see your initials next to those two timings?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: TOMLINS

blocks.text: Okay. So if you could just take us through, please, if you can, that entry and perhaps what some of the nursing references mean or might mean in practice. So we've got:
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "8 am to present [presumably 8.42]: care taken over for the long day."
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes. So care taken over for the 12.5-hour day shift; we called them long days.
blocks.speaker: TOMLINS

blocks.text: You've then got a note to say that [Baby F] was being nursed in Optiflow, 7 litres in air.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes. I was just going to confirm 7 litres of flow via the Optiflow, but no extra oxygen to what any of us were breathing, just 21%.
blocks.speaker: TOMLINS

blocks.text: Okay. You observed:
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "No desaturations."
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Is that right?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: TOMLINS

blocks.text: And you recorded a heart rate around 180 to 190 beats per minute?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: TOMLINS

blocks.text: Can you tell us anything about that sort of heart rate?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, that's quite fast, so that's quite tachycardic.
blocks.speaker: TOMLINS

blocks.text: I can't remember off the top of my head what the normal range... It's slightly elevated in my opinion.
blocks.speaker: TOMLINS

blocks.text: We'll come back to that in a moment. Other observations you've recorded as normal?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: TOMLINS

blocks.text: You've then recorded the fluid allowance, which we understand relates to the administration of something called total parenteral nutrition.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, that's right.
blocks.speaker: TOMLINS

blocks.text: Is this right, that [Baby F] was also receiving lipid and a 10% dextrose solution in addition to that TPN?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, that's what I've got in my statement as well. So the three of them all together would be equal to 165ml per kg per day.
blocks.speaker: TOMLINS

blocks.text: It says "infusing via a long line". We've heard something about a long line. Just in brief, please, describe to us how those three fluids would enter via the same long line.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: It would be -- I can't remember what we called them at Chester, but the long line itself that goes into the baby is just one long really thin white line and then we would have an infusing set, which would sort of divide the fluids into three, so there'd be three different bungs, which we would attach -one would be the TPN, one would be the lipid and one would be the dextrose -- and they could all infuse together via three different ports, if you like.
blocks.speaker: TOMLINS

blocks.text: Okay. Those ports introduce them individually into the same long line?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes. As far as I can remember, that's how we did it at Chester, yes.
blocks.speaker: TOMLINS

blocks.text: Right. You've noted, "Site is satisfactory"; what's that referring to?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Referring to whether there's any redness or swelling or bleeding or signs that it's tissued.
blocks.speaker: TOMLINS

blocks.text: Okay. What do you mean by tissued, please?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: That's the sort of slang we would use for when the line was no longer in a vein -- so the proper word is extravasated, I think. It means the tip of the line is delivering fluid into tissues around a vein rather than into the bloodstream.
blocks.speaker: TOMLINS

blocks.text: Right. And therefore ceasing to be effective?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Oh, sorry, could you repeat that?
blocks.speaker: TOMLINS

blocks.text: And thereby ceasing to be effective; is that right?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Oh yes, that would stop it from working properly, yes.
blocks.speaker: TOMLINS

blocks.text: You put:
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Line very positional."
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Can you explain that, please?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes. Quite often the babies would cause the infusion pumps to alarm for high pressure. Often it was to do with them bending their arm or their leg, so often we would have to put splints on their limbs to try and keep them straight because, yeah, if their arm or leg was bent sometimes the pressure was too high for the fluids to go through.
blocks.speaker: TOMLINS

blocks.text: So does that line mean that the location of the long line was at risk of that sort of problem?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I would say so, yes. Usually they all would have issues with being positional. It was a really common problem, yes, that we used to encounter.
blocks.speaker: TOMLINS

blocks.text: Okay. BM, we understand, is a representation of blood sugar levels.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: TOMLINS

blocks.text: It indicates this morning, 1.7.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes. That's low.
blocks.speaker: TOMLINS

blocks.text: It's very low. And perhaps that explains the next entry:
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Therefore bolus of 3.5ml 10% dextrose currently infusing over 15 minutes."
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: TOMLINS

blocks.text: So is that an attempt to increase, by way of the introduction of dextrose, those sugar levels?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, like an additional extra bolus on top of the fluids he was already having to try and correct it.
blocks.speaker: TOMLINS

blocks.text: So is that in addition to the 165ml of combined TPN, lipid and dextrose solution?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I believe so, yes. As far as I can remember, it was just extra additional.
blocks.speaker: TOMLINS

blocks.text: When it says infusing, is there anything significant in that?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Not that I can recall. It's just (overspeaking) --
blocks.speaker: TOMLINS

blocks.text: How would that additional -- sorry.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Oh sorry. You go on.
blocks.speaker: TOMLINS

blocks.text: How would that additional bolus have been provided?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I imagine through the long line. When I left my statement, I was unable to tell from the notes whether he had any additional peripheral cannulas, I wasn't certain, so I think it was via the same long line as the other fluids, but I can't be sure.
blocks.speaker: TOMLINS

blocks.text: Okay. The next line talks about U&E and SBR. Could you explain that, please?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes. U&E means urea and electrolytes, and SBR means serum bilirubin levels, so blood tests.
blocks.speaker: TOMLINS

blocks.text: Okay. So they were being monitored, therefore taken that morning?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: TOMLINS

blocks.text: "Under single lights with eye mask in situ"?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, that refers to single phototherapy lights. So he already had jaundice, so that would have been why we took the bilirubin blood test. So under one set of lights with eye goggles on just to protect the eyes.
blocks.speaker: TOMLINS

blocks.text: If we could go next, please, to tile 214. We looked at the day before when you'd made one entry. I think if we just scroll to the bottom we can see that perhaps, because you're designated nurse for [Baby F], we can see that you've made effectively all of the entries from the time you came on duty.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, that's right. Yes, 8 am to 7 pm. They were all me.
blocks.speaker: TOMLINS

blocks.text: We've already scrolled up, but we can see -- we have looked at the heart rate the day before when you entered it within the white band. We can see here that from 8 am, I think, which is your first entry, certainly up until 11 o'clock, does that suggest that -- you've recorded 180 to 190 beats per minute in your note and we can compare the numbers there -- that that, did it, continued to be the case from 8 until at least 11 o'clock that morning?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes. Each of those is tachycardic, looking like one -yes, maybe 180 to... It might be 195. It's hard to tell because the numbers don't quite line up with the lines. But yes, I think 180 to 195.
blocks.speaker: TOMLINS

blocks.text: Does the yellow band signify anything in particular?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, the yellow band means the parameters are either above what they should be or below. In that case it's higher than you'd expect.
blocks.speaker: TOMLINS

blocks.text: Okay. We'll come to the period after 12 o'clock a little bit later, but if we can just scroll down again and look at that time between 8 and 11 o'clock.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Respirations within the white line, a little bit raised towards midday again. Would you agree?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes. Sorry, I didn't keep an eye on what column was what, but it looks like they're up around 60 in the middle of the day and then slightly raised again towards the middle of the afternoon, I think.
blocks.speaker: TOMLINS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: TOMLINS

blocks.text: Okay.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Always within normal parameters, but at 3 o'clock almost higher than they should be.
blocks.speaker: TOMLINS

blocks.text: So at the ceiling of what you might expect?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: TOMLINS

blocks.text: If we can move on, please, in a similar vein to tile 215, and look at the right-hand page, please.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: A form we looked at a few minutes ago from your preceding day shift. Again, a form you're familiar with?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, I'm familiar with this.
blocks.speaker: TOMLINS

blocks.text: If we read down, please, to 8 o'clock in the left-hand column, and if we look at that row, that's your first entry for the day shift?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: TOMLINS

blocks.text: We can see in the input column for boluses or bolus, would that represent the dextrose bolus that you discussed in the note and when I asked you about the note?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Are we able to make it a tiny little bit bigger, please, if that's all right?
blocks.speaker: TOMLINS

blocks.text: I'll certainly try.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Thanks. It's a little bit fuzzy.
blocks.speaker: TOMLINS

blocks.text: Someone's nodding behind me so if you can just wait.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Thank you.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Thanks. Yeah, that's better.
blocks.speaker: TOMLINS

blocks.text: Reading across from 8 am -- thank you, Mr Murphy.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: That's your first initial, I think, for the shift on the righthand side?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: TOMLINS

blocks.text: And reading across, in the bolus column, that's in the input side of the form, it appears to be a bolus.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, 10% dextrose, 3ml it looks like.
blocks.speaker: TOMLINS

blocks.text: We can see his blood sugar entered at that time, to the right, of 1.7.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: TOMLINS

blocks.text: Again, consistent with your note that we looked at from 8.40 to 8.42?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, that's consistent.
blocks.speaker: TOMLINS

blocks.text: Just carrying on until that time round about midday, as we go down the columns, is that another bolus at 10 am?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, another 4.3ml at 10 am.
blocks.speaker: TOMLINS

blocks.text: So a larger bolus at 10 am?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: TOMLINS

blocks.text: If we look across to the corresponding blood sugar level.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: 1.3, I think that says.
blocks.speaker: TOMLINS

blocks.text: Yes. And the observations on that level?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Dropped further (inaudible: distorted) than the 1.71.
blocks.speaker: TOMLINS

blocks.text: So he's had 7.3ml between 8 and 10 o'clock --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: TOMLINS

blocks.text: -- without raising the sugar level, as was hoped; would that be right?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: That would be right. I don't know what came first in that column for 10 am, the bolus or the sugar.
blocks.speaker: TOMLINS

blocks.text: I don't know whether we got that sugar of 1.3 and then we gave that bolus or whether we gave that bolus and the sugar -- it's hard to tell based just on this.
blocks.speaker: TOMLINS

blocks.text: I imagine it's probably the blood sugar level and then the bolus.
blocks.speaker: TOMLINS

blocks.text: Okay. So one prompting the other?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I think it would probably be that way round, but it's hard to tell just based on this.
blocks.speaker: TOMLINS

blocks.text: Okay. I'd like --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Sorry, before we leave that, the writing to the right, is that of any significance?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Certainly. There is a figure in brackets, Nurse Tomlins. Does that tell us anything? That's at the 8 o'clock entry, first of all.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Brackets to the 8 o'clock... Ah yes, 1.7ml per kg per hour, I think that says. HR, I think.
blocks.speaker: TOMLINS

blocks.text: I think it says 1.4.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, 1.4, sorry, ml per kg per hour, I think that says.
blocks.speaker: TOMLINS

blocks.text: Okay. What would that refer to, please?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I think that would be the rate at which we -- oh, hang on a minute, I'm in the urine column. That's his urine output, I think, 1.4ml per kg per hour. Because that's written in the column with the urine and where the bowels are opened. So that's what I think that is.
blocks.speaker: TOMLINS

blocks.text: Okay. There's another entry, I'm not sure it's quite as clear, in the 10 o'clock entry that I was asking you about. Can you help us with that at all?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes. So that number there, I don't know if that says 12 or 2ml, and then I've put "discarded mucky". So that was an aspirate from the NG tube. If it was a little bit mucky, we wouldn't give it back, we would just throw it away. But I'm not sure whether that's a 12 or a 2.
blocks.speaker: TOMLINS

blocks.text: Mucky meaning, please?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I can't remember the aspirate, but usually it would look maybe brownish or it would just -- it would maybe not look how you would expect semi-digested milk to look.
blocks.speaker: TOMLINS

blocks.text: Maybe just a bit murky in colour and -- yeah, I can't remember exactly what that particular aspirate looked like, but I imagine it was probably brownish.
blocks.speaker: TOMLINS

blocks.text: All right. Can we go next, please, to tile 217.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Another form, Ms Tomlins, the blood gas record. If we could look at the entries from 5 August, please, on the left-hand side.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Again just concentrating on that period up until around midday, there are two entries on the form, which, reading across, appear for your initials; is that right?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: That's correct, yes.
blocks.speaker: TOMLINS

blocks.text: Indicating at 08.09 the glucose level was 1.7?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, that's correct.
blocks.speaker: TOMLINS

blocks.text: Yes, that's correct.
blocks.speaker: TOMLINS

blocks.text: Despite the two boluses that we've just looked at on the fluid balance chart?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: TOMLINS

blocks.text: We look next, please, to tile 219. For the sake of completeness, that's a prescription for the administration or another infusion of glucose. Do you recognise that type of form?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Vaguely, yes. Not as good a memory of this one because I suppose I didn't write it, so -- but yeah, I do vaguely remember these.
blocks.speaker: TOMLINS

blocks.text: All right. If we scroll down, we can see on the computer certainly you're entered as the user for having administered the glucose; is that right?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, that's right. That's me, N.Toms.
blocks.speaker: TOMLINS

blocks.text: Do the times assist with when that prescription refers to? It's scheduled at 12. It appears to have been administered at 8.30 and then is filed at 12.59. Can we conclude anything from those entries?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I'm just reading the details. Hang on.
blocks.speaker: TOMLINS

blocks.text: Please take your time.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: (Pause)

Yes, I think it means I administered it and [Nurse C] signed it. I'm not sure why it was scheduled for midday, but it would obviously have been something that was meant for right then, so we obviously gave it at 8.30.
blocks.speaker: TOMLINS

blocks.text: If we go back to the carousel, please, and we look at the next tile, 220. Again, another form, is it, that you might recognise from your time at Chester?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, I recognise these.
blocks.speaker: TOMLINS

blocks.text: If we go, please, to the left-hand column and the dates of 5 August. I think the first one is far from the cursor.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, I see that.
blocks.speaker: TOMLINS

blocks.text: Do you recognise your initials or signature in the
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "given by" column?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, that's me, the first one being -- I think we signed it for 10.15, myself and -- I think that's Ailsa Simpson.
blocks.speaker: TOMLINS

blocks.text: Right.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.

blocks.text: Yes.

blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.speaker: OGDEN

blocks.text: It continues below.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.speaker: OGDEN

blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.speaker: OGDEN

blocks.speaker: OGDEN

blocks.text: Sorry, your note continues.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So I say, "Brought to the Resuscitaire", and that's where we would have stabilised him in theatre.
blocks.speaker: OGDEN

blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: It's like the surface, the flat surface with the heat and the gas supply that you would do any sort of resuscitation or stabilisation of the baby on. And there's one of those in the theatre that he will have been born in and we'd have had one for each twin.
blocks.speaker: OGDEN

blocks.text: Okay. Sorry, I interrupted.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Then I've written that he was pink and crying initially and his heart rate was more than 100. blocks.speaker: OGDEN

blocks.text: So is that all the Resuscitaire?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: This is all at the Resuscitaire at birth, yes. I have then written his oxygen requirement increased on the Resuscitaire to about 80%, with the PEEP being given.
blocks.speaker: OGDEN

blocks.text: So even though he was breathing for himself with the oxygen support and the PEEP pressure that we were giving, he was needing more oxygen and because of that I have said my decision was to give surfactant. The only way to give surfactant is through a breathing tube so I have intubated him a size 3 tube, which was put in 7 centimetres at the lips. And then I've documented the capnograph change, which is a colour change if your tube is in the right place and you're getting carbon dioxide breathed out, which is your indicator that the tube is in the right place and that he had equal air entry with the tube in, and we have given 240 milligrams of surfactant.
blocks.speaker: OGDEN

blocks.text: Surfactant is something that babies, premature babies receive to help with their breathing; is that right?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, a lot of premature babies will need that to help their lungs open and close more easily and to reduce the amount of oxygen they need.
blocks.speaker: OGDEN

blocks.text: Then you put "commenced on"?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Commenced on the ventilator at settings of 20/5 and a rate of 40."
blocks.speaker: OGDEN

blocks.text: So the 20/5 are the pressure settings that the ventilator requires. So 20 is the maximum pressure when the ventilator breathes in for the baby and 5 is the baseline pressure, which is the same as PEEP, to keep his lungs open so they don't fully collapse down.
blocks.speaker: OGDEN

blocks.text: Okay. R40?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: A rate of 40, so 40 breaths a minute.
blocks.speaker: OGDEN

blocks.text: Thank you. Then there's a comment about -- is that cannulation?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes. I have written that I attempted to cannulate him -well, attempted to cannulate twice, and I have put by myself and by the SHO, which was unsuccessful, and then I've documented that we had a gas at that time.

blocks.text: Yes, a blood gas.
blocks.speaker: OGDEN

blocks.text: Just briefly take us through those figures, please.

blocks.speaker: OGDEN

blocks.text: Thank you. Carry on, please.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Then I have written, "Decision for UVC", which will be because we couldn't get a cannula in, we still needed some access to give the medications we needed to give.
blocks.speaker: OGDEN

blocks.text: So I have written that a UVC was inserted under aseptic technique by myself and one of the SHOs and that we inserted it to 8 centimetres, that it was bleeding back, which signifies that it's inside a vessel. blocks.speaker: OGDEN

blocks.text: And I have just documented the calculation of how we came to the 8 centimetres, which is a weight-based calculation, so that it needed to go 6.5 centimetres plus the length of the cord.
blocks.speaker: OGDEN

blocks.text: Then some more blood gas results?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.speaker: OGDEN

blocks.text: Right.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: And then the blood sugar has dropped from the previous one but until this point he won't have been receiving any dextrose because he wouldn't have had a line in.
blocks.speaker: OGDEN

blocks.text: And the lactate had come down from that initial one so was coming down towards normal.
blocks.speaker: OGDEN

blocks.speaker: OGDEN

blocks.text: And the plan, please, if we just scroll up.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I have written:
blocks.speaker: OGDEN

blocks.text: "Repeat blood gas in 30 minutes."
blocks.speaker: OGDEN

blocks.text: Because whenever you have a blood gas that's over-ventilated like that, you don't want the carbon dioxide level to stay that low for a long period of time so you want to do very frequent gases until it gets back to normal range.
blocks.speaker: OGDEN

blocks.text: A chest X-ray and an abdominal X-ray would be because the baby was intubated and had a UVC inserted.

blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: OGDEN

blocks.text: Thank you. I think -- did that conclude your dealings with [Baby F], certainly on 29 July?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.speaker: OGDEN

blocks.text: Okay.

blocks.speaker: OGDEN

blocks.speaker: OGDEN

blocks.text: And I don't know what that's in reference to, if that's the femoral pulse on the right or something else because I have not clarified further.
blocks.speaker: OGDEN

blocks.text: It might be in the next line if we go on to the next line.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes. I have written:
blocks.speaker: OGDEN

blocks.text: "The thigh on the right side anteriorly/posteriorly was swollen and full."
blocks.speaker: OGDEN

blocks.text: This thigh was swollen and that his heart rate increased on palpation of that leg.

blocks.text: Right. So if we scroll down again please.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.speaker: OGDEN

blocks.text: was there too. So the plan was to stop the TPN via that long line. To give another bolus of dextrose, to move the TPN to a peripheral line and put a new long line in.

blocks.text: You'd seen through the night a series of similar boluses; is that right?

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: OGDEN

blocks.text: Sorry, again I interrupted, I apologise, I just wanted to cover that. So new long line?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Okay, right.

blocks.text: If we go to perhaps line -- tile 244.

blocks.text: Yes. I have documented at 10.30 that a new long line was inserted into the left foot, so on the other leg, inserted to 15 centimetres via an aseptic technique, and we were awaiting an Xray to confirm the position.

blocks.speaker: OGDEN

blocks.text: Okay. You don't have any recollection of having fitted the long line. Do you have any recollection of what happened to the various fluids that [Baby F] was receiving when the long line was changed?
